notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0149b.stoa023.opp-l: Footnote numerals and stray marks such as (a), (b) have been omitted; the edition's bracketed manuscript readings are translated in parentheses. Line 1: 'Davi l'' read as 'David'; 'videp' as 'video'; 'peum' as 'Deum'. In II, 'Optimum, justum mandare Judicem' is obscure and probably corrupt; rendered tentatively. In III, 'Non minus enim erat impotens' is taken as 'he was not unable'. In IV, 'ex o Deum operatum' appears corrupt (perhaps 'ex eo'), read as 'from the time when'; the Greek word after 'graeca lingua' is garbled in the scan (αναστΐτ<ν) and could not be identified, possibly a word for 'without beginning' or 'unchanging'; it is marked [...].

The second passage (VI) is badly damaged by scanning in its later part; several readings are reconstructed. Notable: 'effici(??)t' read as efficiebat; 'cural(??) ut medicas' as curabat ut medicus; 'humamus compatiobatur' as humanus compatiebatur; 'immortalis mer(??)batur' as moriebatur ('the immortal one died'); 'sublita mestalita(??)' as sublata mortalitate; 'fu(??)rus scilicet mortis mora' read conjecturally as futurus mortis mors ('the death of death'), uncertain; 'in pe(??) hominis et salutem' taken as in perniciem hominis, sense of 'et salutem' unclear; 'sp(??)tes' as sperantes; 'ad (??) revocavit' supplied as 'the world above' (ad superos?), conjectural; 'jam de(??) morte' as devicta morte. Some biblical references are illegible and shown as [..]. In V 'quod Coelum valuit nuncupari' rendered 'which it was proper to call'; 'non praescriberet terra' (the earth should not bar [him]) is a legal term and obscure.

Sections VII and VIII are badly damaged in this scan, with many illegible words; VIII especially is largely fragmentary, and bracketed words there are conjectural restorations from context, while [...] marks what could not be recovered. In VII the reference 'I Patriiii, 24' is printed as given; the quoted verse is I Pet. iii, 21. In VIII the Solomon quotation is cited as Sap. ii, 2 but is Wis. ii, 23. In IX 'Marcix, 39' probably stands for Mark x, 29. In X the reference 'I Petr.xvii' is taken as I Pet. i, 17. In X 'virtutes hujus mundi' (virtues of this world) is odd in context and may be corrupt.

XI: 'ad aedificationem Deificant' is evidently corrupt (perhaps 'Deificam' or 'Dei'); left as [...]. Editorial parentheses (manuscript readings, glosses, scripture references) are translated as printed; footnote numerals omitted. 'Petriii' and similar run-together references read as I Pet. iii etc. XII: 'bacreditaiem' read as 'haereditatem', 'Ador.' as Acts. XII: 'nulli obsequendum' is terse; the sense seems to be that no one is to be obeyed for the sake of temporal reward. XIII: 'puros in malitia' echoes I Cor. xiv, 20 ('be children in malice'); 'consitiis' read as 'consiliis'.

XIV: 'Ita nomen militiae dedisse' lacks a governing verb; taken with 'sciant'. 'circumspector' is obscure (perhaps 'one who looks out for advantage'). XVII: the edition marks a lacuna after 'inobedientia', and the following sentence ('Et quae si nusquam comparentur sibi...') is obscure and probably corrupt; the rendering is tentative. XIX: a lacuna is marked after 'cupiditate'. 'a Deo propter scandalum' is syntactically unclear; '[set apart]' is a guess. 'cohibentibus corruptoribus suis' is obscure: perhaps 'at their corrupters' urging'. In 'Nam qui iracundiam retinet, is magis est continens, quam qui linguam... subtrahit' the comparison may be corrupt; translated as it stands. Scanning errors corrected silently (cerla- mina, vet = vel, rapite = capite, faciet = facie, nou = non, cbaritas).

Line 20: 'continentia genus propinquitatem' is evidently corrupt; rendered by sense as kinship with continence. 'lesles' read as testes (witnesses), 'continentim' as continentiae. The parenthesis 'Si tamen compatimur... ejus' appears to be an editorial/scriptural insertion (cf. Rom. viii, 17; I Pet. ii, 21); kept in parentheses. The editor's conjecture '(fortasse certaminibus)' ('perhaps "struggles"' for 'virtues') is omitted from the text. Line 21: 'Judaeii' read as Jude 2. Line 22: the edition marks lacunae at 'et alienum.... de dilectione sentiendum' and after 'Deus dilectio est....'; sense there is uncertain. The editor's alternative '(fortasse ante omnia)' ('before all things') is omitted. The tract ends at 'profuisse'; the remainder ('Codex, evulgandum censui...') is a fragment of the editor's dissertation, begun mid-sentence, attached to this reference; it is translated as given. Footnote numbers omitted.

nodes.text: THE LETTER OR BOOKLET OF SAINT HILARY.
(The numbers indicate the annotations placed at the end of the letter.)

I. The glorious David says thus in the Psalm (Ps. xviii, 5): Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. From this, then, we are given to understand that, once the sound has been prepared beforehand, that is, the first principles of the Faith, one can arrive at the inmost and more perfect things of the faith, so that, if our first rudiments waver, it may not be said to us by the voice of the Lord rebuking [us] (Luke xvi, 10): If you have not been faithful in a little, who will give you what is greater? But since I see that there is a fixed form, which it is not permitted to go beyond, for the difference between Jews and Greeks, that is, Gentiles, let us first set out the difference (the manuscript codex has: discuss). For I judge that nothing else need be believed by the Jews for the truth of the faith except that Jesus Christ is the Son of God; that through him both the race of Israel is saved and the Gentiles too are baptised in his name; for the rest they know through the Law and the Prophets. But the Gentiles, for whom the labour is real and greater, are to be admitted and taught in this order. And first, indeed, that they withdraw with their whole heart from idols and from all the pleasures of men, so that, when the evils have been cut off and pulled up by the roots, good and religious things can be sown in their breasts: that is, to believe in one God, and to fear him. Next, to know that he himself fashioned all things, and that all things of the world, or which have been made, came to stand by his command, will and making. That there is a body of Scripture; but what need has this of being called the Law and the Prophets, since indeed it was written through men, not by men? For the Spirit of God, who knows all things, inspired holy men to speak, either to destroy depravity, or to build up faith, or to raise hope, or to threaten judgement, or to keep promises. Next, they must believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, through whom God made all things, and without whom nothing was made, through whom we have received that the Word, that is, the reason of the universe, was in the beginning with God. For so the glorious Evangelist John begins, saying (John i): In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. Next, that there is the Holy Spirit, who animated and strengthened all the things which God made through the Word. That there is one baptism, by which men are reborn in God. They must also believe in the resurrection of the dead in the same flesh; [and in] the future judgement of God, in which, according to a man's deeds, either punishments are paid back to the wicked (the manuscript codex has: are repaid), or the appointed rewards of good works are bestowed. So great is the difference between Jews who are converting and Gentiles who are coming to believe: what God is, or of what kind, and how great; who the Son of God was, and of what kind, and who the Holy Spirit [is]: for the Three are one.

II. Certainly it befits your prudence to know this, that we are able both to speak and to know those things about God (the manuscript codex has: this) which either he himself wished to be known about himself among men, or to which man has been allowed, by his permission, to approach. Let man not seek him on earth, nor put him together among images, lest he believe him like to anyone; for true faith has always set forth God thus: not born, not made, incomprehensible, inestimable, invisible and impassible; and therefore the only true God, who begot some things, and made, arranged, ordered and adorned others; best, just, [it is fitting] to commit [things] to [him as] Judge. And therefore every man is without excuse who has not acknowledged his Maker in the time of acknowledgement, since after his departure he will have a just Judge: [every man] who has thought he should be converted not in his own time but after it has passed. These things it is right to believe about God. Whoever has believed these things keeps himself from all injustice. Having done good and just works, he will have eternal rest in life.

III. [As to God] having a Son: do not think that I say he was begotten in the way that men are procreated; but, as it is fitting to believe about God, that God has a Son born indeed from himself, without his substance being divided, nor the substance of his majesty being divided, and so that he should not seem passible on that account. Nor that [the Word] was brought forth from the mouth like our speech, so as to consist of letters and syllables, nor is the Son of God to be held composite and therefore dissoluble. Nor [was he made] from nothing, as the rest of things were made, lest he be joined as like and equal to the others who were made; but as he alone knows who begets, and he who was begotten, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: No one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father (Matt. xi, 27). Likewise we read in the Scriptures: My mystery is mine, my mystery is mine (Isa. xxiv, 16). And truly it is fitting that it be hidden concerning that generation at which no one was present, not even a moment of time. For before the ages, and before anyone could dare to conjecture, the Son of God was born without times, which in the Greek language they call achronos [timeless]; for he is always Son, because [the Father is] always Father: for it is impious to assign to God something afterwards which he did not have before, since God is always perfect. So that even what was fashioned afterwards for our sake was already with him, if not in substance, then in complete design: for he was not unable to make all things at once, but [he did not,] so that all things, ordered and arranged by degrees, might obey according to their rank and honour; and so that they should not remain passive and without honour, with none among them older than another. For if the birth which was undertaken by the Son of God for our sake is incomprehensible, not laid bare to mortals, how much more that one which is known to no one except God the Father and to himself alone? For the angel Gabriel speaks thus to Mary, as the Evangelist testifies: The Spirit of the Lord will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke i, 35). What is overshadowed is hidden, and is not known to all. Therefore, if this birth, which was set down (it seems we should read: arranged) for our sake, is unknown to us, how much more that one which is far removed from us? And why do I say from us, and not from every heavenly creature? Let this therefore suffice, what we have seen, what the divinity wished us to know. Nor should knowledge be stretched further, lest each one be held sacrilegious, whoever has gone beyond the granted (the manuscript codex has: shaken) bounds of knowledge.

IV. We have received, then, that Christ is the Son of God, from the beginning the true Wisdom (I Cor. i, 24, the power of God and the wisdom of God); the Word, that is, the reason; spirit (John iv, 24, God is spirit, etc.); way (John xiv, 6); light (John i, 9, and again iii, 19); arm (Isa. liii, 1, and John xii, 38, And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?); strength; power (I Cor. i, 24); truth (John xiv, 6); bread (John vi, 35, 48); wine (Matt. ix, 17, and John xv, 1, etc., I am the true vine); life (John i, 4, and xiv, 6, and often elsewhere); door (John x, 1, 2, 7, 9); shepherd (ibid., 11, etc.); and very many other things, which are for the sake of men, and all live in him; which each person will learn thoroughly in the course of time as Scripture teaches. If, then, we confess the Son of God as known, we know that through him God the Father created the ages visible and invisible. For it is not right to believe that God began working [only] from the time when the world took the beginning of its coming into being, or that he must be believed to have ceased and left off after the fashioning of the world, since the Lord speaks and says: My Father is working until now (John v, 17). Whoever does not know him to be tireless assigns him idleness either before, or rest afterwards; and he does not know that nothing has ever befallen him, but that he always is, which the Greek language calls [...]; and that he is in all things always perfect spirit.

V. So there are very many things which he made through the Son, of which either only the names are known to us, or not even these are known. For how many thrones are there? How many powers? How many dominions? How many principalities? How many spirits? How many angels? Things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man. How great, too, do we think the brightness is among invisible things? We cannot even estimate it, since among the things that are with us all are worthy of wonder. For among all things, the world too which we behold was fashioned through the Son. And indeed he commanded light to be, and made it, so that other things might become visible; and he gave it the name day (Gen. i, 3, 4). To the darkness he added the name of night (Gen. i, 5). Then he displayed the firmament, to divide between the waters, which it was proper to call Heaven (Gen. i, 6, 7), so that earthly things should not be mixed to sight with heavenly ones, but there should be something to separate the human from the divine. For he had already established out of nothing the very materials from which all the elements were to come into being. After this he commanded the waters to be gathered and come together into one, so that the dry land might be shown (Gen. i, 9). Nor are any of these deprived of names. For he called the gathered waters sea (Gen. i, 10), and he willed that the separated dry land should possess the name of earth (Gen. i, 10). But these seemed insufficiently furnished. So he added to them a kindly fruitfulness, and beauty (Gen. i, 11 ff.). And in a wonderful way he commanded that one to bring forth first which had been fashioned last, not disturbing the order or ignorant of his own work; but he wished the last to have something first, lest it lie last in everything; and he joined the second things to the first, lest the first despise the lower. Thus the Son of God, God the craftsman, at the Father's command governed [things] so that by changing the order he might arrange the disposition better. For he commanded the earth to bring forth all fodder, and trees with their self-renewing seeds (Gen. i, 11, 12), and he adorned heaven with lights, that is, with the Sun, the Moon and the Stars (Gen. i, 14), by which he might show the bounds of day or of night, or instruct countrymen or sailors by signs (ibid. and verse 16). He ordered each of the seas, shut in within the limits of the earth (Job xxxviii, 8, etc.), to bring forth its own living creatures (Gen. i, 20, 21); that is, he had animated the materials themselves with soul, so that they might afterwards lend souls to the living creatures as they were born. But to make the earth more fruitful (the manuscript codex has: he had made) (Gen. i, 24, 25), after fodder, after fruit-bearing trees, after all seeds, he commanded it to cast forth the race of four-footed beasts, of wild animals and of serpents, all living and animate (ibid.). Nor was there delay in all these things, for as soon as God the Father had commanded, the Son, who is power itself, took up the command without postponement; for the work stood ready together with the command. But since it mattered much to make the earthly things fruitful as well, and after the divine things, human ones were lacking, he made man, who should be neither wholly from heaven, nor yet be born again wholly from earth: for he formed the body out of all the clay of the earth (Gen. ii, 7), intending to grant the spirit from heaven (ibid.). And although all things were formed at the Father's command, with the Word obeying, in the fashioning of man the Father himself also came forward as maker, so that the earth might not bar [him] from immortality, if immortal hands constituted man. He also granted that man should bear the image of God on earth, intending afterwards to give the likeness, if the image were kept unharmed. Do not think that this outward form of man was made after the image. Far from it. For who would believe that God, after whose image man was made, has any part which does not hear, which does not see, which does not do all things? For the outward form of man does not see on every side, does not hear on every side, is not powerful on every side. But God is wholly light, wholly eye, wholly ear, wholly a most powerful hand. Do the Scriptures lie, then? Far from it. But that there is something inward in man which is itself also called Man, the apostle Paul teaches us, saying: Though our outward Man is corrupted, yet the inward is renewed daily (II Cor. iv, 16). This is [the one] made after the image of God, whom we call nous (that is, mind), who can be like God then, when he has been proved impassible, unshaken, blessed and holy, and without end (without end: to the end, or, if you like, without unfaithfulness, or in faith). And he gave [him] free will and a capable mind, not without a law of living, lest, being great and loosed from law, he be made equal to all the animals; adding a threat after the law, that if he kept the law he would come into eternity; if he did not keep it, he would bring death upon himself and lose his salvation (Gen. ii, 16). Now the name of the man who was made is Adam (Gen. ii, 19).

VI. But since in all animals both sexes had come forth for procreation (Gen. i, 22 ff.), provision was made for man too, that a woman should be prepared for him also for the sake of generation (Gen. i, 27; ii, 20, 21 ff.); and she was made, as Scripture testifies, and received the name Eve (Gen. iii, 20); and the prescription of an equal law did not separate her either from reward or from punishment. But after God had seen all things made perfect and adorned through his Word (that is, the Son), he handed over into man's power all the things that were with man (Gen. i, 28). When Lucifer saw that all things had been handed over to him, the wretch envied man (Gen. iii, 1, etc.). (For they too are free not to sin, and are permitted to remain in blessedness if they keep the commands.) Through the woman he persuaded [him] to transgress the law and commands of God (Gen. iii, 1 ff.), so that man should become guilty against God's commandments and fall under the sentence (Gen. ii, 17). He was therefore cast out into this world (Gen. iii, 17 ff.); for in Paradise, while he was without sin, he used to dwell (Gen. iii, 23). But since he had begotten men after the transgression, he drew the whole race of men with him all the way to death. Yet there would not be lacking good or just men, since indeed those born afterwards were free not to transgress, and God did not cease daily to admonish [them]. Then the divine goodness and the fatherly kindness provided generously in many ways: first indeed through the just Patriarchs, then through Moses and the Prophets. But all these were dying in Adam. In the last times, lest the Devil should triumph completely (for this is his name since he envied man), and lest man, after the times of condemnation had been fulfilled, should be held long in punishment against the mercy of God, he received the salvation which he earned by [God's] compassion alone. For God the almighty Father sent his Son Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, through whom he had founded all things, not suffering even this to be done without him. Yet no one was fit who could or knew how to bear man patiently (perhaps we should read: take away, that is, from the power of the demon), nor could anyone overcome the powers of this world and of this darkness, or conquer death, unlock the underworld, utterly uproot and destroy the strength and power of sin, except the Son of God, who had been a sharer with the Father in the making of man; who could both hide himself in man, and, as man mingled with God, accomplish and display mighty works; so that through him, our bonds of sin being blotted out (Col. ii, 14), we might be able to approach God the Father reconciled, and made sons of God (I John iii, 1). So the Son of God is sent, and entered into man secretly (Luke i): not because he feared anyone, he who was Lord of all; but so that the Devil should not fear to approach the man who was mingled with God, and so that the Devil should not seem less overthrown by man, if he were conquered without encounter and contest. So from a Virgin, the Spirit of the Lord coming upon [her] and the power of the Most High overshadowing [her] (Luke i, 35), the Nativity of Christ according to [his] manhood was celebrated, and he passed through all ages [of life], so that nearly all might learn God; [and] that all these things had been foretold in the Law and the Prophets, so that a thing wonderful to all should not become unbelievable through suddenness; and that those of the past, whose lot it was not to see this with their eyes, might, if they hoped without doubt in the coming of him who was foretold, escape the contagion of eternal death. Thus, then, God the Son of God, so great and of such a kind, was seen on earth as great and of such a kind as humanity could look upon him. For he who on the mountain, granting an appearance of his majesty and goodness, showed himself to the apostles, when his face shone (Matt. xvii, 1; Luke ix, 29; II Pet. i, 17) so that the strength of the sun seemed to have come forth, and he wore his garment so that it seemed whiter than snow, and yet the disciples, already instructed, already taught, already holy, could not endure the brightness of Jesus, that is, of him who had taken up the vices and sins of all men still to be healed (John i, 29). What if God had come in all his greatness, to show his brightness and power to men? Perhaps all creation, feeble and ready to fall, would have given way. But the Son of God had come to save. So, man in the body he had taken, God in power (John i, 1, etc.), he taught as master (John xiii, 13), persuaded as brother (Matt. xxviii, 10), brought about as God (John xiii, 13), chose as foreknowing (John vi, 74; xiii, 1[.]; xv, 16), healed as physician (Matt. viii, 16; ix, 35; xi, 8, etc.), suffered with [us] as a human (Heb. iv, 15). And now, when all things had been done and fulfilled which either the Law or the Prophets had foretold, or the salvation of man required (John xix, [..], 29 and 30), at the very last the immortal one died by the death of the man (ibid., v. 30), so that, mortality being taken away, he might give immortality to men. So, hung on the wood (Matt. xxvii, 35), with the Jewish people crying out (Matt. xxvii, 23), among whom he had performed such mighty works, so that on it all the envy of the Devil might be overcome (God reigned from the wood), on which the envious one had deceived man, he hastened willingly to death (John iii, 14, etc.; [..], 28, etc.; xii, 31, 32, 33, 34, etc.), being, that is, the death of death; [and] having unlocked the underworld, and having scorned all those things which then had force in the underworld for the ruin and [against the] salvation of man, he illuminated all the just and those hoping in him, and called [them] back to [the world above], showing the Devil and the powers of this world and of this darkness that their wickedness had not prevailed: that they themselves remained in punishment, while man, whom they envied, was set free (the codex has: to man). So man, triumphing with God, death now conquered, no longer mortal, went up to the world above. Thus, then, Christ Jesus our Lord suffered so that he might rise; he rose because he had already suffered; teaching this, namely that whoever has joined himself with God may seem to die, but cannot perish. Yet it seemed too little done for the punishment of the enemies if, having destroyed the enemy, he had given life to man and not added glory. And so that greater punishment might come upon the Devil and his angels, he carried up in triumph into heaven the man, who now had flesh that would not die, to show him to the angels and holy powers (Acts i, 9; Ps. xlvi, 6), offering the liberated man to God the Father as a gift. Soon he sent the Holy Spirit as his deputy in his place (Acts ii, 1, etc.), whom he had promised to the disciples when close to his passion (John xiv, 16 and 17), to be both a help and a sanctification to men who believe. This is the order of our belief concerning Christ.

VII. But since we have now made mention of the Holy Spirit, [it is] to be believed in the Holy Spirit, th[rough] whom all things which were to come about afterwards he both inspired and sanctif[ied], of [one] substance (perhaps 'communication' should be added)..... Th[ese]... three are one, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Next it is to be believed that [there] is baptism, by which men, purified and [made] sons of God, are sealed in faith; by which all sins, whether of birth or of man, were to be cleansed: in which not the filth of the body is laid aside, but of the conscience, [for it] is the asking of a good [conscience] toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (I Pet. iii, 24).

VIII. After these things [faith] requires [belief in] the resurrection of the dead in the same [flesh]. For it is evident, n[or] is it lawful to say otherwise, that God is both [wise] and fore[knowing], and as one wise and foreknowing he chose the better thing, that man, once made, should be eternal rather than not be. But if you think it better that he should not be, [it would have been] shorter [not to make him], before he made him. And that man, who [consists] of body and soul, is eternal, the Scriptures teach us in very many places; but I will set down a few as examples. Solomon cries out, saying (Wis. ii, 23): God created [man] for immortality. Nor without reason in Genesis is man, [after] sin, forbidden to approach the tree of life, lest he live for ever (Gen. iii, [22]), [that is], that he should continue immortal. Who [is this], if not man, who had been made immortal by God, and [would have kept] an immortal body? [I do not] believe this troubles the reader, that man, [driven] from the tree of life by God, [...] and in this [...] to man: for he was already in transgression. [He] therefore [...] this death, which was assigned by God as a remedy, and which comes about through the separation of body and soul [...] and a tearing away [...], if [he had come] to the tree of life; [for] it would have been necessary, by sharing in life [...] eternal, in an immortal [state] [it would have been] necessary to keep [his] sin. Therefore this too [was done] deliberately, that [...] [...] [...] of God, [...]. Therefore al[ways] [...]. But [when] we die, [...] the reason is grasped: not [that] man [perishes], but [that he] is separated; nor [that the things] from which the body was built [are lost], but [that they] are reserved for the day of [resurrection and] judgement. For it is not right that anything should be lacking to God when he judges, since it is certain that God's judgement [comes] after the end of this [age]. [And] this too must be [instilled]: that the whole man must also be [raised], since [all] will be found to be either in [good] or in [evil]. And this [so] that those who have done well according to his will may be re[warded], and [the wicked] may be destined for eternal punishments. Hence let us seek the lawful precepts, [shunning] what is contrary, [and] obeying [...].

IX. Now therefore [let us speak] of [rank]. In rank two [things] are to be held: the poor man and [the rich]. And to the rich of this world indeed it must be commanded (I Tim. vi, 17): not to be [high]-minded, nor [to trust] in the uncertainty of their riches, but in the living [God], who provides us abundantly with all things for [the enjoyment of our] work; [to be] rich, but in [good] deeds, sharing, treasur[ing up] for themselves [a good foundation] in [the future], so that they may lay hold of how good life is. Next, [that they should know] that [riches] have not been received and are to be held, and [trusted in], so that [they may serve] them. And let them not despise the poor, nor make [riches] a ministry of wickedness or an instrument of lust, nor [think] them handed over to themselves on their own account, nor [deem] them anything but [what] may be lost. [Let them] know [that they are] appointed by God as stewards of the grace of God, so that in the distribution their [good] will, or [their] depraved [will], may be known; so that they may know that, through abundance, a greater temptation has come to them, unless they have been wise. Let them learn to pay out riches. But let them distribute their means with a view to immortality, so that they may be like God: merciful; let them not be judged lavish squanderers of the Lord's property. And let them do these things with confidence, and with cheerfulness. For Paul the apostle says (II Cor. ix, 7): God loves a cheerful giver. Let them not think that what is spent on the needs of the poor in regard for the commandments of God can come to an end, since [riches] were both received from him and are necessary, and he is accustomed to supply them profitably and to increase them. For how can temporal things be lacking, when on account of them, if they are paid out well, eternal things have been promised and prepared? He who is Christ speaks more truly, saying (Matt. xix, 29; Mark x, 29): Whoever leaves for my sake house, or farm, or parents, or the rest, will receive a hundredfold in this world, and in the future eternal life. And if some assign this to the time of persecution, I nevertheless hear our Lord admonishing thus: that whenever, at any time, his commandment has been fulfilled for his sake in any holy work, the appointed reward will not be lacking. Let us not be anxious. God takes care of us. The prophet cries out, saying (Prov. xxii, 2, and more explicitly Wis. vi, 8): I made both the poor man and the rich, and I have equal care for all. God takes care: and does anyone fear that his patrimony will be diminished, from which payment is made at God's command? Let us rather fear lest, if we have been fearful and barren and faithless in good works, we be judged needy and destitute. Let us rather fear to be filled with sadness, for concerning rich men of this kind, though in the person of one, [Scripture] in the Gospel nevertheless referred to all together, saying (Matt. xix, 22): But when he had heard, he went away saddened, for he had many possessions. Let [the rich man] not fear that he will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty (ibid., vv. 23 and 24). Rather let him be humble, let him be generous, so that from this he may be judged more blessed, [since] he will feel want neither in this world nor in the future. Let him give to the poor, so as to lend to God: let him reckon God his debtor (Prov. xix, 17). Let him know that mercy is set above sacrifices. He will attain glory and rest if, from these riches in which others are judged both corrupt and lost, he receives the crown, the fruit of justice and mercy.

X. But the poor man must be consoled in such a way that he knows that in considering poverty [there are] greater goods for him. And first indeed, that it was profitably provided for him by God: that God in his foreknowledge considered his weakness, and determined that he could not bear the burden and anxiety of riches. Next, let him perceive how many temptations and how many dangers he has passed by on account of poverty. Abundance is lacking, which is often harmful; yet in poverty he passes the more quickly, without hindrance, to the riches of the soul. Let him consider, surely, what evils he has been spared. He is free of envy, rivalry, plots, deceit, pride, strife, and those things which riches usually stir up for a man in the world; for with the flow of goods, as with the plenty of supplies, the soul is loosened, the vigour of the mind is broken, the strength of the body is enervated. But in poverty there are no wanton banquets, no shameful drinking bouts: all is sober, all is strict, all is humble, not abject, since they are full of a pure conscience and of virtue. He does not abound in outward means: he is just. The rich man does not easily come to the riches of the soul, that is, the virtues of this world. For he who says (Matt. xix, 24) that it is harder for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven certainly means that it is easier for the poor man. Lest he think himself, on account of poverty, a stranger to God's care, the prophet testifies, saying (Prov. xxii, 2; and more explicitly Wis. vi, 8): I made both the poor man and the rich, and I have [equal] care for all. For God is not a respecter of persons (Acts x, 34; I Pet. i, 17). Nor does he declare that he takes care only for him who is strong in the riches of the world, but for all; and he bears care for the poor too, about to reward the one he finds either humble in riches or patient in poverty. A distribution, as it were, of the whole human body is made, and the service of each [member] is required. Let him consider that the body of a man is indeed one body, but many members. Are all [members] an eye, or a foot, or the other members (I Cor. xii, 14)? But, as Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, says (I Tim. ii, 7): The members which are lower, on these we bestow greater honour (I Cor. xii, 23). And just as the virtue of the individual members is shown in their own order and function, so in the body of the whole human race Poverty and Riches are placed as members, as it were, so that the patience of the poor man and the kindness of the rich man may be proved by God's examination. The poor man ought to rejoice and give thanks to God, because he has been set free from the many bonds of a patrimony. On the day of trial he is not weighed down by the fetters of possessions; the disciple follows the Lord more easily as a free man, entangled in no bonds. Let just mercy toward the needy also not be lacking from him, as far as he can (Tob. iv, 8), because, just as the rich man is made just by generosity, so the poor man is made just by frugality, if he pays out to those lower than himself and to those who have nothing. Let him not fear that he himself will run short, since in the practice of holy stewardship he has a most ready will: nothing will be lacking; the Spirit confirms [this] through the prophet (Prov. x, 3): God does not kill the soul of the just man with hunger. And the Lord in the Gospel (Matt. vi, 33): Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you. Let him not desire to become rich in this world, lest he acquire very many evils for himself, as the glorious Paul says and admonishes (I Tim. vi, 8): Having then food and clothing, let us be content with these. But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many desires, which plunge men into perdition. Rather, if he has chosen to believe with true faith and for the sake of salvation, let him strive after heavenly riches for himself and acquire them, which each person acquires and takes up by [deeds] of justice and mercy and other good acts. Eternal things are to be preferred to temporal, stable things to perishable, more secure things to anxious, free things to dangerous, more glorious things to dishonourable. By these admonitions let both the rich man be moderated and the poor man be relieved.

XI. Now let us speak of sex. That sex is male and female, that is, man and woman. And the man, after the things we have set out above, must also keep this along with everything else for the ordering of a better life: that he love his wife as Christ loved the Church (Eph. v, 25); that, managing all things with one mind (the manuscript codex has: that in every kind with one mind), being in harmony, they may duly pray to God about all things, lifting up pure hands without anger and dispute (I Tim. ii, 8); but let all things be done for edification [...]. Next, [he must] keep the bond of union with modesty and shared chastity, and come together only when there is thought of procreation, or when it does not take away the time of prayer (I Cor. vii, 5). By that prayer I mean the one which is celebrated with the whole ministry of the sacraments and with communion. The rest is supplication and adoration, confession and intercession (I Tim. ii, 1), and vows, all of which have their own times. It is fitting, then, for a man to pray with his head uncovered (I Cor. xi, 4 and 7), not with long hair (ibid., v. 14); his gait should be simple, not swaggering or affected, so that he shows that he has believed not only in word, but also offers to others the pattern of his life. For it belongs to every man to act as priest to God (I Tim. ii, 8). And so he must show his conduct to be most pure, both in catechism (that is, in instruction) and also in lay life, so that even if at the time (so it reads in the manuscript codex) he does not perform the office and duty of a priest, he may yet be made equal to the priesthood by the likeness of his life. But the woman should learn to be obedient to her husband (Eph. v, 22), even calling him lord (I Pet. iii, 6); and she should indeed revere all men, yet serve her own: for the head of every woman is the man (Eph. v, 24). Let her also know how to live chastely with her husband (Tit. ii, 5), which he too should do in every way, so that he knows no other woman besides his wife (I Cor. vii, 1, 5, etc.). For he must know the times for coming together, and abstain from union when it is the time of prayer, or when the woman is suffering [her monthly course], or when she knows she is within the time of purification after childbirth. For God did not join marriage for unchastity, but so that it might serve procreation. Let her learn to bring up children piously (I Tim. v, 10: if she has brought up children), to be modest, not quarrelsome, not given to wine (Tit. i, 7; Col. iii, 18; Eph. v, 22; I Pet. iii, 1), not proud towards her husband (Gen. iii, 16; and Tit. ii, 3, 4, 5: subject to their husbands; and I Tim. ii, 12: nor to have dominion over the man), even if she appears greater in patrimony; but also to go out modest in gait, not with a painted face (I Tim. ii, 9 and 10; I Pet. iii, 3), nor surrounded with gold or costly clothing, nor to busy herself with curling her hair, but as befits Christian women who profess chastity not only in words but through good conduct (I Pet. ii, 12; iii, 1, 2). Let her know that she must keep silent in church; for it is not fitting for them to speak (I Tim. ii, 11 and 12; and I Cor. xiv, 34). [Let her know] that she must be obedient not only to her elders and to the priests, but also to all the brethren (I Pet. iii, 15). Nor [should she] set herself above any man on account of her sex (I Pet. iii, 7), since, when she has fulfilled all things lawfully, she too will be brought to completion in the perfect man (Eph. iv, 13). Rather let her strive for the virtue that will attain glory; not held back by the weakness of her sex, in holiness and virtue of mind, and in all continence and devoted suffering, let her be made equal to the most righteous men.

XII. Now let us take in hand the discussion of the ages [of life]. And first I think infancy should be deferred in teaching, because, whether by the nature of the time or of the age, it cannot take in the teacher's word. And in the case of all those to whom, through lack of age, precepts cannot be given [that bear] on malice and natural innocence, the parents must be bound to admonish them; although, as their age advances, the Church will not be wanting, nor will it cease from admonishing. To boys, however, this must be instilled first: that they should not be absent at any time of hearing, because everything cannot be fully taught at once. Next, that they join innocence to simplicity, so that they do not prolong their boyhood in persistence in malice. Care and watch must be taken that they are not corrupted in the other ages. To their natural goodness let them also add the good and divine gift of faith, so that they may persevere always good, always holy, always innocent, always the work of God and not of nature, by the handing on of belief. They must consider that, in order to remain chaste or modest, they ought to come to church more often, because they need to be strengthened more often, admonished more often, since for them, on account of their still less stable age, the Devil's attack will be heavier. They must observe all things with fear, and above all beware of fornication, which holds the beginning of idolatry; and whoever has followed the one must necessarily know the other. How then is he understood to believe and to have left the Gentiles, if he returns to the things which the gentiles practise? Let them indeed be obedient not only to their parents (Col. iii, 20), but also to all who are older in age (I Pet. v, 5), provided that their admonitions and speech bring no unlawful hindrance. Let them reckon that they have God as Father (Matt. vi, 9); they ought to hope for his inheritance (ibid. and v. 10; Acts xx, 32; Rom. viii, 17; Col. iii, 24), which consists not in temporal things but in eternal ones. Indeed, if God foresees that it is useful for them, he will grant temporal things too, especially when he sees each one pursuing eternal things, as his Son, our Lord, says (Matt. vi, 33): Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you. Hence no one will doubt that an abundance of necessary things on earth will not be lacking to those for whom heavenly things are prepared (ibid. and v. 34). Therefore, since these things are to be hoped for from God, no one is to be obeyed [for their sake]; rather, all are to be obeyed because God wills it, not because any reward ought to be hoped for from that person in this life, but because we strive to fulfil God's lawful commands even in these things (I Pet. ii, 13). Lastly, they are to be congratulated if they have come to God at the very first beginning of free will, devoting their whole age to the good of faith: because [they have] not spent their age in error, so as afterwards to have something to grieve over, but while still boys and innocent they came to obtain from God not so much pardon as grace.

XIII. The young men, however, are to be admonished in this way: if they have wives, let them be taught to live chastely with their wives. Let them know that it is wicked to touch another man's [wife] (I Cor. vii, 1). In this he will give proof and evidence that he has truly renounced his past life, if, after he has believed, there is a reform of his life for the better. For then he ceases to be a gentile and begins to be a Christian, if, carefully keeping all things of the law, he shows himself chaste and modest (I Cor. vii). But if they do not have wives, they must be bound either to have [one] or to restrain themselves altogether, so that they do not think the same things lawful for them which they did before (Col. iii, 5; Eph. v). They must know that they have renounced the Devil, not in words but in deeds. Let them be admonished and know that fornication and adultery are forbidden; that it is lawful to touch no woman except one's wife, and she taken in a godly way. Therefore either they must marry a wife (I Cor. vii, 9: let those who do not contain themselves marry), or embrace continence. Yet lest, frightened, they put off faith, let them know that it is bad not to believe on account of impurity, [but] worse to be found unchaste after they have believed. The young must consider how to surpass their age in all their deeds, strong in mind and virtue, and, young in the inner man (II Cor. iv, 16), be placed among the old with God as judge (I Cor. xiv, 20). They are also to be congratulated because, not having spent their whole age, but in the very heat of their years and in adolescence itself, they have renounced the Devil, author of disgraceful deeds, and unclean acts; and, renewed, they show themselves to God pure in malice (ibid.): young in temptations, in counsels and thoughts grave old men. And I think all these must be admonished to obey all for God's sake (I Pet. ii, 13), to learn to rule their household well (I Tim. v, 4), [and], if they have children, to treat them piously (ibid., v. 10; Tit. ii, 4) and instruct them in divine things: for these are the signs of our faith, if we have not only believed, but have also handed on to others what we have believed.

XIV. Let the soldiers of Christ know that they must be watchful in peace and most brave in persecution. [Let them know that they have] so given their name to the military service, and so hope for the donatives or pay of eternal life, that, besides the daily contests of peace which we wage against the Devil, whom we have renounced, we should be mindful of the fight and battles of persecution. Bodily punishments are not to be feared; rather, the rewards or promises are to be considered. It is captivity rather, and slavery under the enemy, and exile from the heavenly Homeland, and the Judgement of God, as well as the mockery of the foe, and eternal death, and eternal torments that are to be dreaded. Let us consider that we are all mortal and that we must necessarily die. How glorious and praiseworthy [it is], if what must necessarily be suffered is overcome in glory. All speech is to be fitted to the destruction of idolatry and to the praise of the martyr's crown, so that the soldier of Christ may go forward armed in every way to overcome the enemy and to repel his darts. Let the one who preaches the gospel be asked what he does. If he is a soldier or an official, or a judge (the manuscript has 'or'), [let him be told] to be moderate. A countryman, not to grumble. A townsman, not to be sly or watchful [for advantage], and not to exercise his wits in bad things. A trader, not to perjure himself. A farmer, not to hoard the grain supply. A craftsman, not to deceive or cheat.

XV. Now faith, as the apostle Paul defines it (Heb. xi, 1), is the substance of things which we hope for, and the evidence of things which we do not see. One ought to believe, and in faith, that God is able also to fulfil what he has promised, and to transfer one's hope into the future. And then, full of faith, one will be able to reach most easily the things that have been promised (Heb. xi, 1). Faith sets invisible things before our eyes. Having entered upon it, we abandon all the things of the Devil, and of the powers of this world and of this darkness (Eph. vi, 11, etc.); we draw near to God with confidence. For it is necessary to believe and hope for what God has commanded, when we renounce what the Devil had implanted.

XVI. Hope follows faith. Therefore let us speak about it. Hope, then, is the expectation of all the future things which we hold in faith, through which we are saved, as the apostle Paul writes (Rom. viii, 24): For we are saved by hope. But hope that is seen is not hope. For what a man sees, why does he hope for? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it through patience. Hope has fear within it: I do not mean that fear which whoever lives in faith ought to forget and cast out, but that which is one of the spirits with which Jesus is filled, as Isaiah testifies (Isa. xi, 1): A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from his root, and there shall rest upon him the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him: that spirit of which David sings, saying (Ps. xxxiii, 10): Fear the Lord, you his righteous ones. Whence they are also made blessed, as the same [David] declares and says (Ps. cxi, 1): Blessed is the man who fears the Lord. He speaks of that fear which is chaste and pure. For the fear of the Lord is chaste, says David (Ps. xviii, 10), enduring for ever and ever. Therefore fear too is twofold, and one is to be sought and the other shunned. The fear to be sought, then, is the admonition and safeguard of all the things which we believe or hope for: for let us fear the Judgement, because we hope; and let us dread the Lord, because we believe him to be a mighty Judge.

XVII. But since the fear of God is chaste, and chastity is a species of continence, we must now treat of continence and its virtues. Continence, then, is the restraint of all bad things that are desired. I added 'bad' so that judges might not think this definition applies in common to good things and bad. For he who holds himself back from good things is not rightly continent; but he who [holds himself back] from bad things [is] rightly so. But indeed in all precepts there ought to be a twofold consideration and teaching. And I think this should be retained and observed in other matters too, that when you have treated one part, you should know its contrary; and the very ordering of things requires that, when you have held to one part, you must abandon the other. We find indeed that evil had no substance from the beginning, since disobedience..... evil is set over against good (Ecclus. xxxiii, 15). And if they are nowhere compared with each other, it is preserved by the protection of the good.

XVIII. Continence, therefore, is to be taught and kept in bad things. In good things eagerness is to be demanded. David declares and teaches, saying (Ps. cxi, 1): Blessed is the man who fears the Lord: he will desire greatly in his commandments. Likewise, that one ought to be continent in bad things and desirous of good things he warns in another psalm, saying thus (Ps. xxxiii, 14): Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceitful things. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace, and you will attain it.

XIX. It seems good also to discuss the continent: for I see many who are continent only with respect to conjugal union, and in all the other parts of continence worse than the Gentiles. For if you consider, very many of them are both irascible and drunken, and insolent, and proud, and, from a kind of appearance of continence, rather puffed up: violent men, slanderers, greedy, swollen, much pleased with themselves, so that you would rather judge that the very continence which they profess to have has supplied tinder and flame and fuel for crimes. Whereas surely these things in which we are daily rebuked are to be cut away first, and then the virtue of continence is all the more to be kept in all other vices; and for perfection it is not union that is to be rejected, but modesty that is to be preferred. For when the apostle Paul was admonishing the churches, he did not enjoin a uniform continence, but warned in which things it is to be sought and found, saying: That she may be, he says (I Cor. vii, 34), holy in body and in spirit: defining that he is not continent who has not been proved most continent in both parts. [I see] many, or very many, so burning with desire..... as the outcome shows, that they would rather endure every kind of punishment, or undergo any sentence of the Church whatever, than give up their intimate living together: not knowing that God, foreknowing, said of such people (Matt. v, 28): Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Such people cannot excuse their fault [by saying] that they have not directed their eyes to lust, when they both lie together and under one roof, or sleep in one bed. Hence, when rebuked, they profess to do this spiritually, applying to strangers names of affection or of family devotion. Indeed, since we understand the substance of the Devil also to be spiritual, it ought to be added: but of spiritual wickedness and malice (Eph. vi, 12), [set apart] from God, to the scandal and ruin of the Church: since they cannot be torn away from it either by persuasion, or by the prohibition of the elders, or by fear of a present sentence or of the future Judgement: whereas quite often even those whom lawful marriage has joined a slight quarrel separates. What evil is this? What evil an inseparable love, that they cannot be separated from affection for those of another blood? It is shameful to say what they are not ashamed to do. Certainly they are not free even from the kiss, which is the pledge and earnest of the serpent. Indeed, when you have rebuked them, they at once bring out these words: that the integrity of their body can be proved; whereas integrity of mind is to be required of them first, although they cannot be fully examined even in body. For it is not permitted to men to know or lay bare the hiding places of the conscience, as Scripture says (I Kings xvi, 7): Man sees in the face, but God in the heart. God alone beholds inward and secret things. But plain is the voice of the Lord warning (Matt. vii, 20): By their fruits you shall know them. If you consider what their look is like; with how troubled a brow, how shamelessly they gaze about; how much boldness in the face, how much assurance they carry; in some an immodest adornment, and an affected gait in display of boastfulness. And the devotion, so to call it, of such a profession goes so far that, on account of the name of virginity, which alone they bear, they become desirable. Hence it is that they make themselves known when they ought to have hidden themselves, offering their service only to God, from whom modesty hopes for reward. So, having crossed the threshold of the house of God, they begin their prayers with uncovered head, interpreting the Apostle (their corrupters restraining [them]) as having made his ruling about married women, not about virgins: not knowing that everywhere he names males of any age 'men', [and] designates all females by the term 'woman'. I know that I have digressed from the proposed treatise on continence; but necessarily, so that henceforth all people of either sex, taught in full continence, may know both from what they should abstain and what they ought to guard: or, if someone has been an observer of continence in one species, in some one kind, and when admonished will not go on to the others, let him not boast that he is in the number of the continent, lest through obstinacy he seem to lose even that part in which he was applauding himself. Therefore he who is taught continence and wishes to approach it ought not to seek continence only in the body or in one part of the body, but ought to recognise the observances of continence in every motion of the mind. For he who restrains anger is more continent than he who withdraws his tongue from abuse, from cursing, from detraction, from lying, from perjury, and from the other evil affections of the tongue. He, finally, who checks his very thought from all wickedness and denies it to every iniquity, is fully continent, and him I do not compare with men, but recognise as most like the holy angels.

XX. Now we must speak about patience and all its good things. Patience, then, is the bearing of all injuries and sufferings, and the enduring of all waiting without haste. Whoever understands it and has it carries the heavy things contrary to life and holds fast to all good things. It has hope for a sister. Yet I explained above that all good things are akin to one another. For it suffers willingly because it hopes, and it bears what is to be hoped for. What is not hoped for is borne impatiently, and [so it is] when nothing is hoped for. But patience bears with all its strength what is recognised when hope is perishing. And if the fruit of patience follows hope, it rejoices in faith as its mother, has God for its helm, and has kinship with continence. Hence the just, while they do all things with patience (Rom. v, 3 and 4), are made glorious witnesses of God, while they are found full of faith, anxious with the fear of God, disciples of continence, and sons of hope with wisdom as their guide. Then [they become] co-heirs of Christ, while they imitate him even to death (if indeed we suffer with him, etc., let us follow his footsteps) in the virtues of patience.

XXI. But now let us discuss justice. Justice, then, is the most equitable distribution of individual things and persons. Whoever holds it and adheres to it keeps his life rightly ordered and without disturbance. He guards equity in all things. He knows what he owes to God, what he should render to the saints and to his equals, what he should not deny to the powers of this world, what he should keep for himself, what is due to his neighbour, and what he should grant to strangers or what befits them. For it is just to worship and love God with the whole heart, and with the whole soul, and with the whole strength; to honour the saints and one's equals; to pay taxes to the powers (Rom. xiii, 7); not to be proud, but rather gentle and humble (I Pet. iii, 13 and 14); to love one's neighbours as oneself (II Tim. iii, 2); not to pursue strangers and enemies with hatred, but to love them; to be subject to those who came before, or to those greater in age (I Pet. v, 5). For the Lord too, though he was lord of all, was baptised by John, because John was before him in birth among men (Luke vii, 28), and he declares that in this way all justice is fulfilled (Matt. iii, 15). From this mercy is born, and godly obedience is produced. Whoever is found in all these things is not undeservedly said to abide in Christ (I John ii, 6), since Christ himself is all these things. The glorious Paul teaches and instructs us about Christ, saying (I Cor. i, 30): Who is for us from God justice, and sanctification, and redemption. Likewise in another place (Jude 2): Who is mercy, peace, and love, which the Greeks call agapē. Let us now pass on to it, because in all things it is the greatest among the others. So the blessed Apostle declares (I Cor. xiii, 13): But these three remain, Faith, Hope, Love.

XXII. Love, then, is the bond of souls, chaste, sincere, and without rivalry. Charity is the fulfilment of all the commandments. It is the force of all the precepts; whoever has it has everything; without it, one remains bad and imperfect. And so that your prudence may know how much charity is worth, let us read the Lord's answer in the Gospel: when he was asked, he spoke thus (Matt. xxii, 37): You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two precepts the whole law hangs, and the Prophets. You see that in this alone all the heads of the law hang. Truly, whoever has it can now be called a god and a son of God. Consider that by this alone you are like God. Does he who loves God hope? Does he fear? Does he trust? No: he only loves. God, says Paul (Rom. viii, 3), when he had loved the world, sent his only son in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that by sin he might condemn sin in the flesh. Hence Paul too sets it above all good things, saying (I Cor. xiii, 1): And if I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I am nothing, and like a ringing bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have faith, so that I move mountains; and if I distribute all my goods as food for the poor; and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, I am nothing. Charity is magnanimous. Charity is kind. Charity is not jealous, is not puffed up, does not act wrongly, is not provoked, is not confounded, does not seek its own, does not think evil, does not rejoice over injustice, but rejoices in the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things. Charity never fails. Therefore whoever wishes to find out this, as it were, species must unlock the whole of Scripture for himself: the whole law must be opened, all the Prophets made known, all the virtues, acts and commandments of Christ made known, and the teaching of the Apostles opened thoroughly and taught. And although all the species we have treated above are beyond men's grasp for a full treatment, much more so is that in which they are all fulfilled and on which they hang; especially since John the Evangelist has forbidden us in his Epistle to dispute [about it], when he teaches that it is both the Son of God and God the Father, saying thus (I John iv, 8): God is love. If anyone can speak of the whole of God, he can also [speak] of love, which is God. Therefore, if it is sacrilege to dispute about God more than is permitted, to be silent is religious; and [it is] foreign.... to think about love. For [one must think] as much about it as about God, since God is love.... Let each one therefore know himself; for if anyone has love in himself, he is a dwelling-place of God, because God, who is love, abides in him. It is fitting now to bring the species to an end in the fullness of love and of all good things, especially since all have been gone through again; or if anything has been passed over, let it be seen to be included in the fullness of the world. Before all, I beg pardon from your people with most sincere holiness, that your Holiness, whose way has been proved more skilled and more holy by God, may deign to correct, reshape and supply whatever my mediocrity has either passed over or, having found, could not explain more fully; or, if you approve, since the little work was begun by us at your request and completed with God's help, that it lacks nothing, that you keep me in remembrance in your holy prayers as well as those of all the brothers. And let the rivals of my faith know that an account has been given, and recognise that it agrees with the Church, and let them rather take up the mystery, so that we may rejoice not only to have believed, but also to have been of some small profit to enemies and believers. ... the codex, I thought it should be published. But since I deny it to Hilary of Poitiers, if you wish to assign it to another Hilary (which I for my part allow), assign it to Hilary of Arles, who we know for certain both built sacred churches (a), and therefore dedicated them, and delivered not a few sermons to the people (b); and also that he was accustomed to cite passages of Scripture from the Vulgate translation, which indeed the author of this Sermon uses (c). And this conjecture and suspicion of mine is strongly favoured by the very style of Hilary of Arles, quite similar to the style of this Sermon. But to whomever this sermon is finally assigned, it is certainly praiseworthy, and without doubt ancient, and therefore one that deserved to recover its ancient form and original brightness.
